the decision rule: accept when NPV is positive, reject when negative
the mechanics: each future cash flow discounted back to today, then the upfront cost subtracted, with original arithmetic
the discount rate as the hurdle: firms discount at their cost of capital (sibling topic, reference only)
why NPV matters: it compares projects of different sizes and timings fairly on one today-dollar scale
the limits: the answer is only as good as the cash-flow estimates and assumptions

the two reasons cash flows are discounted: time value of money and risk (CFI)

claims.claim: Working definition: net present value is the difference between the present value of a project's expected cash inflows and the present value of its cash outflows (OpenStax 16.2; Investopedia); CFI frames it as the value of all future cash flows over the entire life of an investment discounted to the present. This lesson's working definition: the present value of a project's expected future cash inflows minus its cost today.

The upfront cost is part of the calculation: the initial investment is a cash outflow at time zero — the purchase price paid today — subtracted from the discounted inflows, not added to them (CFI's formula; OpenStax's NPV = PV inflows − PV outflows with the year-zero outflow in the Sam's Sporting Goods example).

Decision rule: projects with a positive NPV should be accepted and projects with a negative NPV should be rejected (OpenStax); positive-NPV projects are worth undertaking and negative-NPV ones are not (Investopedia); a positive NPV creates value while a negative NPV destroys value (CFI).

Mechanics: calculating NPV is a time value of money problem in which each future cash flow is discounted back to its present value and the initial outflow is then subtracted (OpenStax); CFI's formula discounts each period's cash flow at the discount rate and subtracts the time-zero outflow.

The discount rate acts as the hurdle: CFI calls it the required rate of return or hurdle rate and discounts project cash flows at the firm's WACC or the appropriate hurdle rate; Investopedia says the discount rate may be a hurdle rate based on a company's cost of capital; OpenStax uses the firm's cost of funds as the discount rate in its worked example.

Cash flows are discounted for two reasons: the time value of money — money is more valuable the sooner it is received because it can be invested and earn a return (CFI) — and risk, with riskier investments receiving higher discount rates (CFI; OpenStax notes the discount rate can be adjusted for the riskiness of a project's cash flows).

NPV makes projects comparable: it accounts for the timing of each cash flow, which can have a large impact on present value (CFI), and it can be used to compare different projects (Investopedia), putting projects of different sizes and timings on a common today-dollar scale.

Limits: NPV relies on a long list of assumptions, is sensitive to small changes in them, can be manipulated to produce a desired output, and assumes a constant discount rate over time (CFI); it relies heavily on inputs, estimates, and long-term projections (Investopedia); and it can be difficult for a non-finance audience and problematic when capital is limited (OpenStax).
A negative-NPV project may still show accounting profit, but because its expected return is below the discount rate it is considered to destroy value (CFI).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does NPV account for project size?
positions: Investopedia lists as a con that NPV does not consider project size or return on investment — it measures total value added, not value per dollar invested.
CFI and OpenStax treat NPV as the standard value-added measure, and Investopedia itself notes NPV can be used to compare different projects.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that NPV puts projects of different sizes and timings on a common today-dollar scale, and honestly notes in the limits that it measures total value, not efficiency per dollar invested.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 16.2: Net Present Value (NPV) Method
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2024-02-08) because openstax.org blocks direct fetch. Supports: NPV as the difference between the present value of cash inflows and the present value of cash outflows; the equation NPV = PV cash inflows - PV cash outflows; positive NPV projects should be accepted and negative ones rejected; calculating NPV as a time value of money problem in which each cash flow is discounted back to present value; the firm's cost of funds (9% in the worked example) as the discount rate; spending money today in the hopes of making more money in the future; the discount rate adjustable for the riskiness of a project's cash flows; disadvantages including difficulty for non-finance audiences and problems when capital is limited.
